title: Is the Bible Reliable Enough to Build a Life On?
excerpt: The evidence can show that the Bible we have is very nearly the Bible that was written and that its writers stood near the events, and it cannot show that what they wrote is true, which is a different question and the harder one.
body:
A student comes home from her first semester with three facts nobody at church had told her. The original manuscripts of the Bible are gone. The copies that survive differ from one another in hundreds of thousands of places. And a story she has loved since childhood, the woman caught in adultery, sits in her own Bible inside brackets, with a note saying the earliest manuscripts don't have it. At the same table her uncle answers with a number he once read on a card, thousands of manuscripts, more than for any other ancient book. He has begun to suspect that it doesn't answer what she asked.

Down the hall of a hospital a third person is reading a psalm at three in the morning because there is nothing else left to hold. For her the question is not academic. She wants to know whether the thing in her hands will bear weight.

The question has two halves, and most of the confusion comes from treating them as one. The first is whether the Bible we have is the Bible that was written, and whether its writers were in a position to know what they report. Evidence can speak to that. The second is whether what it says is true. The first half can be settled a long way at a desk, and the second cannot be settled there at all.

## The Case Against

The skeptic's case is old, and its best form has four parts.

The first is the copying. A pagan critic named Celsus made the charge in the second century: some Christians, he said, "have corrupted the Gospel from its original integrity, to a threefold, and fourfold, and many-fold degree, and have remodelled it, so that they might be able to answer objections." The modern form is more exact. No original of any biblical book survives. The earliest pieces of the New Testament are fragments whose dates are argued over, and the oldest complete copy comes from the fourth century. Scholars estimate the differences among the Greek manuscripts in the hundreds of thousands, against about 138,000 words in the Greek New Testament itself.

The second is the distance. On the dating most scholars hold, Mark was written around the year 70, Matthew and Luke between about 75 and 95, and John in the 90s. That is forty to sixty-five years after the crucifixion. None of the four names its author in its own text. In the meantime the stories were passed on by word of mouth.

The third is that the accounts disagree. Matthew says Judas took his own life and the priests bought a field with his money; Acts says Judas bought the field and fell headlong in it. Luke ties the birth of Jesus to a census under Quirinius, which the Jewish historian Josephus places about ten years after the death of the Herod in whose reign Luke also sets it. The first three Gospels and John appear to differ on the day Jesus died.

The fourth is the collection itself. Thomas Paine put it bluntly in the 1790s. Nobody can know, he wrote, whether the church's collectors "added, altered, abridged, or dressed them up," and in the end "they decided by vote which of the books out of the collection they had made, should be the WORD OF GOD, and which should not." On this telling the Bible is the anthology of the party that won.

## What Is True in It

Nearly all the facts in that case are correct, and Christians ought to be the first to say so.

The originals are gone. The count of variants is right. The woman caught in adultery and the last twelve verses of Mark are missing from the oldest complete manuscripts, and most scholars, believers among them, think neither was part of the book as first written. The dates are the usual ones. The Gospels' titles were almost certainly not written by their authors. The census in Luke is an open problem, and the site's page on it says of Luke that on the evidence historians can weigh "he may have" gotten it wrong. The common way of fitting the two accounts of Judas together adds what neither text says. No single act ever closed the list of books for every church, and Protestant, Catholic and Orthodox Bibles still differ in the Old Testament.

It is also true that Christians have defended the Bible badly. The comparison with other ancient books has often been made with stale figures and uneven counts. And the student should have heard about the brackets from her own church before she heard about them from anyone else.

## What the Manuscripts Can Show

The picture behind the first charge is a game of telephone, one whispered message passed down a single line with no way to check it. The copying of the New Testament did not work that way, and the difference is the reason the charge fails.

The text was written, so a copyist could look back at the page in front of him. The copying branched, so that by the late second century copies were being made in Egypt, Syria and Italy by people who never met. A mistake made in one branch travels down that branch and no other, and when the branches are laid side by side it stands out. Older copies were not thrown away when new ones were made. And the early Christians themselves compared copies and argued about them. Around the year 180 Irenaeus knew that some copies of Revelation gave the number of the beast as 616, and he said which reading stood in the oldest copies. Origen answered Celsus directly: he knew of no one who had altered the Gospel except the followers of three teachers he named, Marcion first among them.

This is also why the number of variants is so high. Every slip in every copy counts, so a book that survives in thousands of copies will have thousands of slips. The first six books of the *Annals* of Tacitus survive in a single medieval manuscript, and that manuscript has no variants at all. Its errors are simply invisible. Most of the differences among New Testament manuscripts are spelling, word order and accidents no reader of English would notice. The places where the wording is really in doubt and the sense changes are a small share. They are known, and they are marked in the notes of nearly every modern Bible. The brackets in the student's Bible were printed there by scholars, a great many of them believers, who found the problem and reported it.

The manuscripts can therefore show a good deal. The wording of the New Testament can be known about as well as any ancient text's can, and better than most. Editions made by different teams with different convictions agree on the great bulk of it.

The limits are just as real. The first decades of copying can't be seen by anyone. No method could detect a change made to every copy before the earliest one that survives. The additions that are known did not manage to spread to every branch even in the second century, which makes a sweeping early change unlikely, though it has not been proved impossible. And the whole comparison answers only one question. Scholars have a well-attested text of Homer, and nobody concludes from that that Zeus is real.

## What the Dates Can Show

A gap of forty to sixty-five years sits inside a single lifetime. People who had known Jesus were still alive when the first Gospel was written. And the Gospels are not the earliest Christian writings. Paul's letters come from the 50s, and in one of them he hands on a summary he says he was given: "that Christ died for our sins in accordance with the Scriptures, that he was buried, that he was raised on the third day in accordance with the Scriptures, and that he appeared to Cephas, then to the twelve" (1 Corinthians 15:3–5). Most scholars, including many with no stake in Christianity, think that summary took shape within a few years of the events. He adds that most of the five hundred who saw the risen Christ "are still alive" (1 Corinthians 15:6), a remark that invited checking.

Luke says how he worked. He had "followed all things closely for some time past," drawing on "those who from the beginning were eyewitnesses," so that his reader "may have certainty concerning the things you have been taught" (Luke 1:2–4). The Gospels are ancient biographies, a kind of writing that claimed to report what a real person said and did while arranging material freely and giving speeches in the writer's own words. That explains many of their differences in order and wording. It doesn't explain all of them. Honest readers still hold more than one account of the day of the crucifixion, and none of the solutions to the census has won general agreement.

So the dates show that the writers stood near enough to know. They can't show that everything was handed on faithfully, and the kind of book a Gospel is doesn't prove its reports true. Historians trust accounts of Alexander the Great written four centuries after him, and they trust them critically. The length of a gap matters less than what stood within it, and what stood within this one was a living community that included the witnesses.

## Who Chose, and What Was Dug Up

Paine was wrong about the vote. The Council of Nicaea in 325 dealt with the teaching of Arius, the date of Easter and twenty rules of church order, and nothing that survives from it mentions the books of Scripture. The emperor Constantine ordered fifty copies of the Scriptures for his new city and named no books. The four Gospels and the letters of Paul were being read as Scripture from Gaul to Egypt by the late second century, long before any emperor was a Christian. The edges were argued for much longer. In the 320s the church's own historian still listed James, Jude, 2 Peter and 2 and 3 John as disputed, and the first list that matches the present New Testament exactly comes from a bishop's letter in 367.

Paine was right about something. The churches did judge books partly by whether they agreed with the faith already received. Whether that judgment was sound depends on which faith was there first, and the evidence for that is Paul's letters of the 50s. Two essays on this site take up [who decided what books are in the Bible](/writing/who-decided-what-books-are-in-the-bible) and [whether it can be trusted](/writing/why-trust-the-bible).

Archaeology is where believers are most tempted to claim too much. From the ninth century before Christ onward, inscriptions cut by Israel's neighbors and enemies name kings and events the Old Testament records: Omri of Israel on a Moabite stone, the "house of David" on a stele found at Tel Dan in 1993, Hezekiah shut up in Jerusalem in the annals of an Assyrian king. Where those sources overlap with the Bible they agree on the main facts and differ in detail, as independent sources do. For earlier periods, the patriarchs, the exodus, the conquest, the evidence is thin and argued over. The site's page on [what archaeology shows](/questions/old-testament/what-archaeology-shows) gives the limit in a sentence: "Claims of proof and claims of disproof both say more than archaeology can." A spade can confirm that a king reigned. It can't turn up a covenant.

## The Step Evidence Cannot Take

Suppose all of it is granted. The text is close to what was written, the writers were near the events, and the setting is real. None of that makes the message true. A sincere witness can be mistaken, and an accurately copied claim can still be false. The New Testament doesn't pretend otherwise. It stakes everything on an event and says what follows if the event did not happen: "if Christ has not been raised, your faith is futile and you are still in your sins" (1 Corinthians 15:17).

What the reliability of the text does is narrower, and still worth having. It takes away an excuse. Nobody can honestly say that we cannot know what the first Christians claimed, or that the claim was invented centuries later by a council. They claimed, within living memory of the events and at the cost of their safety, that a crucified man had been raised and that he was Lord. A reader has to decide what to do with it.

Christians have been candid about how a person comes to answer. The Westminster Confession lists the arguments that can move someone to a high view of Scripture: the testimony of the church, the weight of its subject, the agreement of its parts. Then it says where assurance comes from: "our full persuasion and assurance of the infallible truth, and divine authority thereof, is from the inward work of the Holy Spirit, bearing witness by and with the Word in our hearts." A skeptic may hear that as a retreat from evidence. The confession means it as an admission that the evidence can bring a person as far as the door and can't make him go through it.

Jesus said something close to this, and he put the test where few people expect it. "If anyone's will is to do God's will, he will know whether the teaching is from God or whether I am speaking on my own authority" (John 7:17). On his account some of the knowing comes after a person is willing to do what he hears, and cannot be had before.

## Where Christians Differ

Christians who confess that Scripture is God's word still describe its truthfulness in more than one way. Some hold, in the words of a statement written in 1978, "that Scripture in its entirety is inerrant, being free from all falsehood, fraud, or deceit," and that this is said strictly of the original writings, which "can be ascertained from available manuscripts with great accuracy." On this view a real error in any matter Scripture affirms would be God's error, and God does not lie. Others confess that Scripture is wholly trustworthy and cannot fail in what it was given to do, which is to teach the way of salvation and the life of faith, and they hold that its incidental details of number and date belong to the human languages and eras God chose to use. The first group fears that a Bible allowed small errors will soon be allowed large ones. The second fears a faith so tied to the date of a census that one discrepancy can bring it down, as it has for many students. The site's study of the subject treats this as a second-order question that stands very near the foundation. What both confess is that Scripture is God's authoritative word and that it bears true witness to Jesus Christ.

## What We Have Done With the Book

The harm done here is mostly ours. We have oversold the evidence, and people who trusted us found out. We have said that archaeology proves the Bible, and it cannot do that. We have forced the accounts into agreement where the honest answer was that the question is open. We have kept the brackets and the footnotes from our own people, so that they first learn of them from someone who hopes the news will end their faith. A church that hides what is in the margins of its own Bible has told its young that the book can't survive being looked at.

And we have defended a book we do not read. Jesus said to men who studied the Scriptures closely, "You search the Scriptures because you think that in them you have eternal life; and it is they that bear witness about me, yet you refuse to come to me that you may have life" (John 5:39–40). They searched the text and would not come to the person it spoke of, and people who believe every word of it can do the same.

## Enough to Build On

Is it reliable enough? That depends on what a person means to build. For a house of certainty in which no question is ever left open, nothing in history is reliable enough, and no one lives that way about anything else that matters to him. For a life, the evidence gives this much. The words are very nearly the words that were written. The writers stood within reach of the events. Past that point a reader has to trust or refuse, as he does with every person he has ever relied on.

Jesus ended his best-known sermon with two builders. "Everyone then who hears these words of mine and does them will be like a wise man who built his house on the rock" (Matthew 7:24). The other man heard the same words and built on sand. The same storm came to both houses. In the story the difference between the two men is that one of them did what he heard, and Jesus says nothing about how much evidence either had weighed.

The woman in the hospital corridor will not learn at three in the morning whether Quirinius held an earlier office. What she can do is put her weight on the words and find out whether they hold. The student's questions deserve every hour she gives them, and most of them have better answers than she was told. When she has them, the book will still be open on the desk, and it will still ask her for more than her agreement.

*"Lord, to whom shall we go? You have the words of eternal life."* (John 6:68)

*"Everyone then who hears these words of mine and does them will be like a wise man who built his house on the rock."* (Matthew 7:24)
